body_md: HTTP is stateless request-response over TCP. Client sends method, path, headers; server returns status plus body. HTTPS adds TLS. Keep requests idempotent where possible and cache GETs.
code:
GET /feed?page=2 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.ferrisfeed.dev

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
hook: The one protocol every design builds on.

quiz.explain: Because servers don't store client conversation state between requests, you can freely place a load balancer in front of hundreds of identical stateless worker nodes.
options: HTTP holds open dedicated TCP sockets tied to specific server session caches
Because each request carries complete context, any backend instance can handle any incoming request
HTTP requires continuous WebSocket connections to preserve client identity
Statelessness restricts HTTP exclusively to static file downloads
quiz.q: Why is the stateless nature of HTTP considered a fundamental advantage when scaling web architectures?

takeaway: Design stateless handlers that scale horizontally.
trap: Storing session in server memory breaks scaling.

body_md: REST uses resources plus verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH merges, DELETE removes. Return 201 with Location on create, 404 for missing, 409 for conflicts. Version via /v1.
hook: Resources, verbs, status codes — done right.

quiz.explain: REST treats system entities as nouns in URLs and leverages standard HTTP method semantics to express the action being performed.
options: It uses standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on clean noun-based resource URIs
It encodes action names directly into URLs like /getUser or /deleteItem using GET
It bundles all operations into a single POST endpoint with custom action codes
It ignores standard HTTP status codes in favor of custom JSON status flags
quiz.q: How does idiomatic REST architecture map client interactions onto system entities?

takeaway: Name resources as nouns, act with verbs.

body_md: gRPC uses Protobuf over HTTP/2 with streaming. Define service in .proto, generate stubs, get typed clients in any language. Great for internal microservices needing speed and contracts.
output:
protoc emits typed Feed client + server stubs (any language)
ListPosts: unary RPC; StreamPosts: server-streaming RPC

quiz.explain: gRPC combines Protocol Buffers serialization with HTTP/2 multiplexing, producing strongly-typed, low-latency binary streams ideal for service-to-service calls.
options: It sends uncompressed JSON payloads over HTTP/1.1 connections
It transfers verbose XML envelopes over an FTP transport channel
It leverages Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 for strict schema contracts and compact binary streaming
It passes untyped text strings over raw operating system sockets
quiz.q: What architectural characteristics make gRPC the preferred communication protocol for internal microservices?

takeaway: Use gRPC for fast internal service calls.
trap: Exposing gRPC directly to browsers without gateway.

body_md: GraphQL lets clients request exactly fields they need in one query. Server defines schema and resolvers. Solves over-fetching but needs query cost limits and persisted queries to avoid abuse.
hook: One query, exactly the fields you want.
output:
{"data": {"post": {"title": "...", "author": {"name": "..."}}}}
// exactly the requested fields, one round trip

quiz.explain: Clients dictate their exact data requirements in a single query, preventing over-fetching of unused fields and under-fetching that requires cascading round-trips.
options: It enforces rigid, monolithic server-side responses that cannot change
It forces every device to download full database rows regardless of screen layout
It wraps payloads in SOAP envelopes for legacy enterprise compliance
It allows the client to request precisely the fields it needs in a single round trip
quiz.q: What core problem does GraphQL solve that traditional REST endpoints often struggle with in client applications?

takeaway: Choose GraphQL for flexible client-driven reads.

body_md: WebSocket upgrades HTTP to full-duplex frames. Handshake once, then both sides push. Ideal for chat and presence. Add heartbeats, resume tokens, and horizontal sticky or pub/sub fan-out.
hook: One handshake, endless push both ways.
output:
101 Switching Protocols -> socket open
send({"t":"hi"}); each inbound frame -> render(data)

quiz.explain: After an initial handshake, WebSockets keep a lightweight TCP socket open where both client and server can push messages instantly without the overhead of HTTP headers.
options: They repeatedly trigger HTTP GET requests every second to check for updates
They upgrade the initial HTTP connection into a persistent, full-duplex TCP channel for instant bidirectional push
They use legacy FTP connections to sync chat transcripts in background intervals
They run over SMTP email queues to guarantee message persistence
quiz.q: Why are WebSockets preferred over standard HTTP polling for live collaborative applications like chat or real-time feeds?

takeaway: Use WebSockets for low-latency bidirectional push.
trap: No heartbeat so dead peers linger.

body_md: SQL gives ACID, joins, and schema; NoSQL gives flexible scale-out for keys, docs, or wide rows. Choose Postgres for relations and transactions, Dynamo-style KV for massive simple lookups.
hook: Relations vs scale — pick by query pattern.
output:
CREATE TABLE
// posts(id, author_id, body) ready; writes ACID, PK-indexed

quiz.explain: Relational engines shine when complex data integrity and multi-table joins matter most, while NoSQL stores trade ad-hoc joins for horizontal scale and high-throughput point lookups.
options: Use SQL when you need relational joins and strict ACID transactions; use NoSQL for massive key-value or document scale
NoSQL should always replace SQL for all modern applications without exception
SQL databases cannot scale horizontally under any circumstances
SQL and NoSQL have identical consistency, schema flexibility, and scaling characteristics
quiz.q: What primary architectural trade-off should guide your decision between a relational SQL database and a NoSQL store?

takeaway: Model queries first, then pick the store.
trap: Storing graphs in relational joins at depth 5.

body_md: Redis is in-memory with strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams. Use for cache, counters, leaderboards, and rate limits. Persist with AOF+RDB and cluster when memory exceeds one node.
code:
SET post:42 1 EX 3600
ZADD leaderboard 950 user:7
GET post:42
hook: Memory as a data structure server.

quiz.explain: Keeping data structures directly in RAM allows Redis to handle cache lookups, rate limiting, and real-time counters at tens of thousands of operations per second.
options: It is an immutable disk-bound archive designed for cold document storage
It directly replaces relational SQL databases for all transactional bookkeeping
It serves in-memory data structures like sorted sets and hashes with sub-millisecond latency for caching and real-time state
It is primarily an operating system utility for managing backup tape drives
quiz.q: Why is Redis widely used as an auxiliary layer in high-throughput architectures?

takeaway: Put hot, ephemeral, or ranked data in Redis.
trap: Treating cache as source of truth without TTL.

body_md: Load balancers spread traffic: L4 by connection, L7 by URL/header. Algorithms include round-robin, least-conn, and consistent hash. Health-check backends and drain before deploy.
hook: No single server should feel famous.

quiz.explain: Load balancers continuously ping health-check endpoints, routing incoming requests only to responsive servers using algorithms like least-connections or round-robin.
options: It routes all traffic to a single designated primary server until it crashes
It distributes incoming requests across healthy worker pools and drains nodes that fail health checks
It relies solely on public DNS lookups without monitoring backend server status
It caches all database mutations locally to bypass backend application code
quiz.q: How does an intelligent load balancer protect backend systems during traffic surges?

takeaway: Balance plus health-check for resilient tiers.

body_md: CDNs cache static assets at edge PoPs near users. Origin sets Cache-Control, CDN serves hits in ms. Use versioned URLs for immutable assets and purge on deploy for HTML.
code:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
# app.abc123.js cached at edge
output:
Edge HIT: app.abc123.js served from PoP in ms
immutable -> no revalidation for 1 year

quiz.explain: By serving pre-cached static assets directly from an edge server in the user's local region, round-trip times drop from hundreds of milliseconds to single digits.
options: It hosts primary database replicas directly inside user browser caches
It executes long-running financial database transactions at edge endpoints
It is restricted solely to video streaming and cannot serve scripts or images
It caches static assets at edge Points of Presence geographically close to the end user
quiz.q: What role does a Content Delivery Network (CDN) play in reducing global latency for static web assets?

takeaway: Cache immutable assets at the edge.
trap: Caching personalized HTML at edge leaks data.

body_md: Latency vs throughput: latency is time per request, throughput is requests per second. CDN and caching cut latency; horizontal scale and batching raise throughput. Measure p95, not averages.
hook: Fast once vs fast often — different fixes.

quiz.explain: A speedy average can mask the fact that 5% of your users are enduring 10-second stalls or gateway timeouts due to queue buildup or garbage collection pauses.
options: Because averages hide tail-end spikes where high-intent users experience severe freezes and timeouts
Average latency and tail latency always remain mathematically identical
Averages reflect the absolute worst-case scenario experienced by mobile devices
Throughput increases automatically whenever average latency rises
quiz.q: Why is monitoring p95 or p99 tail latency more crucial for user experience than tracking average latency?

takeaway: Track p95 latency and max throughput separately.

body_md: Polling vs push: short-poll wastes requests, long-poll holds open, SSE streams one-way, WebSocket is bidirectional. Choose SSE for feeds, WebSocket for chat.
code:
const es = new EventSource("/events");
es.onmessage = (e) => console.log(e.data);
output:
HTTP 200 text/event-stream held open
// each server event -> console.log(data); one-way push, no polling

quiz.explain: SSE operates over standard HTTP and is lightweight for unidirectional feeds and live ticker updates, while WebSockets excel when continuous two-way communication is needed.
options: Always use short-polling because persistent connections overload modern operating systems
WebSockets should always be chosen because SSE has been deprecated in modern browsers
Use SSE when you only need one-way server-to-client streaming; use WebSockets when the client must also stream upstream
Never use HTTP-based protocols for any real-time data streaming
quiz.q: When choosing between Server-Sent Events (SSE) and WebSockets for real-time updates, which criterion is decisive?

trap: Polling a feed every second from a million clients.

body_md: API pagination: cursor-based with `after_id` scales, offset breaks on inserts. Return `next_cursor` and limit. Order by indexed (created_at, id) for stable pages.
code:
SELECT * FROM posts
WHERE id < $1 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;

quiz.explain: When new items are inserted at the top of a feed, an OFFSET query shifts rows across page boundaries causing duplicate or missed items. A cursor like WHERE id < :last_seen stays rock solid.
options: OFFSET pagination is immune to newly inserted rows shifting items between pages
Cursor pagination queries against an indexed identifier, preventing skipped or duplicated items when new posts arrive
OFFSET pagination requires loading the entire database table into memory on every request
Cursor pagination removes the need to index database columns entirely
quiz.q: Why is cursor-based pagination preferred over classic OFFSET pagination for infinite feeds like FerrisFeed?

takeaway: Paginate by cursor on indexed columns.

body_md: Caching levels: browser, CDN, LB, app, Redis, DB. Cache-aside reads Redis then DB on miss. Set TTLs, version keys, and invalidate on write. Stampede-protect with singleflight.
code:
val = redis.get(k)
if !val:
  val = db.load(k)
  redis.setex(k, 300, val)
hook: Every layer can save your database.
output:
1st call: miss -> db.load(k), SETEX k 300
later calls: Redis hit in ms, zero DB load

quiz.explain: The application remains in control: it queries the fast cache, fetches from the primary database on a miss, and writes the freshly loaded value into cache for future requests.
options: The application checks the cache first, loads from the database on a miss, and populates the cache with a TTL before returning
The database continuously polls the cache to backfill missing entries
The cache automatically contacts the database in the background without application knowledge
Cache misses throw an unrecoverable exception and force the client to retry
quiz.q: In a cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern, how does the application handle a cache miss?

takeaway: Read cache first, fill on miss with TTL.
trap: No TTL causing permanently stale reads.

body_md: Status codes matter: 2xx success, 301/304 redirect/cache, 400 bad input, 401 unauth, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 429 slow down, 5xx server fault. Retry only 429/5xx with backoff.
output:
Client waits 2s (Retry-After), retries with backoff
// retry 429/5xx only; 400-class means fix the request

quiz.explain: HTTP 429 indicates that rate limits have been exceeded. Obeying the Retry-After interval prevents cascading stampedes on an already stressed server.
options: Immediately spam the endpoint with concurrent requests to bypass the restriction
Treat 429 as a permanent 404 Not Found error and delete local user data
Assume the request succeeded and proceed as if an HTTP 200 OK was received
Respect the rate limit, wait for the specified duration, and retry with exponential backoff and jitter
quiz.q: How should an API client respond when receiving an HTTP 429 status code with a 'Retry-After' header?

takeaway: Signal precisely so retries behave correctly.
trap: Returning 200 with error JSON breaks tooling.

body_md: Monolith vs microservices: start modular monolith, extract when teams or scale demand. Microservices add deploy freedom but need discovery, tracing, and versioned contracts.
hook: Modular first, distributed when it hurts.

quiz.explain: A modular monolith offers rapid iteration and frictionless refactoring. Distributing boundaries across network services is only justified when organizational scale or distinct scaling profiles require it.
options: Immediately deploy microservices to maximize infrastructure complexity from day one
Start with a well-structured modular monolith, separating into distinct services only when team boundaries or scaling bottlenecks emerge
Monolithic architectures cannot scale beyond 100 concurrent users under any configuration
Network calls between microservices carry zero latency, zero failure risk, and require no monitoring
quiz.q: When architecting a new product, what guideline helps determine whether to start with a monolith or microservices?

takeaway: Split by team or scaling pressure, not hype.
trap: Distributed monolith with all the costs, none of the gains.
